```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r}
library(adempR)
```

Bias, coverage and MSE are only meaningful when the estimate and the truth
refer to the same quantity. A common error is to compare a method's
estimate with a parameter of the data-generating model that the method
does not target. adempR makes the target explicit: every estimand declares
its population, conditioning set, effect type and scale, and methods
declare which estimands they target.

## Conditional and marginal odds ratios

In a logistic model with a prognostic covariate,

$$\operatorname{logit} P(Y = 1 \mid A, X) = \beta_0 + \beta_A A + \beta_X X,$$

$\beta_A$ is the conditional log odds ratio given $X$. Because the odds
ratio is not collapsible, the marginal log odds ratio for randomized $A$,

$$\operatorname{logit} E\{P(Y = 1 \mid A = 1, X)\} - \operatorname{logit} E\{P(Y = 1 \mid A = 0, X)\},$$

is smaller in absolute value than $\beta_A$, even without confounding. An
unadjusted logistic regression estimates the marginal quantity; an
adjusted one estimates $\beta_A$. Judging the unadjusted estimate against
$\beta_A$ would report a bias that does not exist.

The marginal truth has no closed form. Following Naimi, Benkeser and
Rudolph (2025), we compute it by Monte Carlo integration over a large
sample of $X$ and report its own standard error.

```{r}
scen <- sim_scenarios(n = 500L, b0 = -1, bA = 1, bX = 2)

marginal_truth <- sim_truth_mc(function(scenario, n) {
  x <- rnorm(n)
  p1 <- plogis(scenario$b0 + scenario$bA + scenario$bX * x)
  p0 <- plogis(scenario$b0 + scenario$bX * x)
  m1 <- mean(p1); m0 <- mean(p0)
  # delta method SE of logit(m1) - logit(m0)
  g <- p1 / (m1 * (1 - m1)) - p0 / (m0 * (1 - m0))
  sim_truth_value(qlogis(m1) - qlogis(m0), se = sd(g) / sqrt(n),
                  method = "Monte Carlo integration with delta method SE")
}, n = 2e5)

estimands <- list(
  sim_estimand("marginal_lor", truth = marginal_truth, effect = "marginal",
               scale = "log_odds_ratio", population = "trial population",
               conditioning = "none"),
  sim_estimand("conditional_lor", effect = "conditional", scale = "log_odds_ratio",
               population = "trial population", conditioning = "X",
               truth = sim_truth_exact(function(scenario) scenario$bA)))
```

Each method lists the estimands it targets and, where useful, declares its
effect type. `sim_validate()` rejects a method whose declaration does not
match the estimand it is evaluated against.

```{r}
methods <- list(
  unadjusted = sim_method(function(data) {
    f <- glm(y ~ a, binomial, data = data)
    sim_estimate("marginal_lor", unname(coef(f)["a"]), se = sqrt(vcov(f)["a", "a"]))
  }, estimands = "marginal_lor", declares = list(marginal_lor = list(effect = "marginal"))),
  adjusted = sim_method(function(data) {
    f <- glm(y ~ a + x, binomial, data = data)
    sim_estimate("conditional_lor", unname(coef(f)["a"]), se = sqrt(vcov(f)["a", "a"]))
  }, estimands = "conditional_lor",
  declares = list(conditional_lor = list(effect = "conditional"))))

study <- sim_study("noncollapsibility",
  aims = "Show that marginal and conditional log odds ratios differ",
  scenarios = scen,
  generate = function(scenario, context) {
    x <- rnorm(scenario$n); a <- rbinom(scenario$n, 1, 0.5)
    y <- rbinom(scenario$n, 1, plogis(scenario$b0 + scenario$bA * a + scenario$bX * x))
    data.frame(y, a, x)
  },
  estimands = estimands, methods = methods, measures = c("bias", "empse", "mse"))
run <- sim_run(study, replications = 200, seed = 11,
               path = file.path(tempdir(), "noncollapse"))
sim_truth(run)[c("estimand", "truth", "truth_se", "truth_method")]
```

The marginal log odds ratio is well below 1. Both methods are close to
unbiased for their own estimand:

```{r}
s <- as.data.frame(sim_summarise(run))
s[s$measure == "bias", c("method", "estimand", "value", "mcse", "mcse_total")]
```

`mcse_total` adds the Monte Carlo error of the truth to that of the
estimates. More outer replications reduce `mcse` but not `truth_se`; only a
larger truth sample (`n` in `sim_truth_mc()`) does. For measures that
compare each estimate with the truth (for example coverage), the summary
also reports a sensitivity range: the smallest and largest value of the
measure while the truth moves over two of its standard errors in either
direction, including points inside that range where coverage changes.

Had we evaluated the unadjusted estimates against $\beta_A = 1$ the bias
would be

```{r}
e <- sim_results(run)$estimates
mean(e$estimate[e$method == "unadjusted"]) - 1
```

which is entirely an error of the evaluator, not of the method.

## Other kinds of truth

* `sim_truth_exact(fun)`: closed form.
* `sim_truth_numeric(fun, error)`: deterministic numerical integration,
  with a stated numerical error.
* `sim_truth_mc(fun, n)`: Monte Carlo, with a standard error; computed once
  per scenario from its own random stream and cached in the run directory.
* `sim_truth_dataset()`: the truth differs between data sets (for example
  a sample average treatment effect). The generator returns it with
  `sim_data(data, truth = list(...))`; methods never see it unless they are
  declared oracles.
* `sim_truth_unknown()`: no truth. Measures that need one (bias, MSE,
  coverage) are reported as unavailable; others (empirical SE, mean SE,
  width, rejection) are still computed.

Only scalar estimands are supported in this version. Vector and functional
estimands (for example survival curves) can be studied as several scalar
estimands at chosen time points.
